questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weave and paint film on canvas
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a lifting paint film on canvas fails along the weave.
questions.stem: During a survey of a colonial storehouse, the team finds a painted canvas whose paint film has lifted in strips that follow the weave. Which property of the support explains this?

options.text: The canvas weave is a texture the paint grips, so the film separates along the threads.
The canvas is woven so loosely that the paint has nothing at all to hold onto.
options.misconception: misreads a lifting film as a loose weave

options.text: The threads contain oil that dissolves the binder within the paint film.
options.misconception: invents a solvent action in the canvas threads

options.text: The weave expands faster than the paint, so the film is torn away from the support.
options.misconception: claims the fabric alone tears the film loose

questions.explanation: Paint grips the weave of the canvas, so a lifting film separates along the threads and leaves strip-shaped losses. A loose weave, a solvent in the thread and fabric-driven tearing do not explain that pattern.
questions.hint: Think about the texture the film is attached to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of sizing on the open weave of a canvas.

stimulus.body: The field laboratory records that the ground on the surveyed canvas contains 40 percent chalk and 60 percent glue by weight, and that the linen beneath it was sized with a diluted solution before the ground was applied.

questions.stem: From the laboratory record above, which effect does the sizing produce on the canvas?

options.text: It fills the open weave so the ground does not sink through the cloth.
It makes the canvas fibre completely waterproof against rain and spray.
options.misconception: treats the size as a waterproof coating

options.text: It binds the chalk particles together so the ground cannot be brushed away.
options.misconception: confuses the size with the binder in the ground

options.text: It stiffens the cloth so the canvas can carry a heavy impasto layer.
options.misconception: claims the sizing stiffens the cloth for impasto

questions.explanation: Sizing soaks into the threads and closes the open weave so the ground sits on the cloth instead of dropping through it. Waterproofing, binding the chalk and stiffening for impasto are not what the size does.
questions.hint: Think about the open spaces between the threads.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the binder limits a day of work in egg tempera.
questions.stem: In the survey tent a conservator must plan a day's work on an egg tempera panel. Explain how the binder limits what can be done in one sitting.

answer.exemplar: Egg tempera binds with water and dries almost at once, so a stroke that is not placed within minutes will sit on a tacky, half-set film and tear the layer beneath it. The painter can therefore lay only a small passage at a time and must keep the day's painting matched to the dryness of what came before. The same quick set means each passage has to be judged and fixed while it is still workable.

questions.explanation: Because egg tempera dries almost at once in water, a passage cannot be adjusted once it has begun to set, so only a limited area can be painted and matched at a time. Long working sessions and the slow corrections possible in oil are unavailable.
questions.hint: Think about how quickly the binder sets.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the interval between touch-dry and full dryness of an oil film.
questions.stem: A conservation survey records that an oil paint layer reaches touch-dry in 6 hours and full dryness after 72 hours. How many hours of further curing remain after the paint first feels dry?
questions.explanation: Full dryness at 72 hours minus touch-dry at 6 hours leaves 66 hours of further curing. Adding the two figures would give 78, and reading the 72 hours as minutes would give a quite different answer.
questions.hint: Subtract the touch-dry time from the full drying time.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the stage represented by a layer exposed in losses.
questions.stem: A survey team photographs a panel on which the finished colours cover a grey-green layer visible in six losses of paint. Which stage does that grey-green layer represent?

options.text: The underpainting, laid first to establish the light and dark masses of the design
The final glaze, applied last to deepen the shadows of the finished picture
options.misconception: calls the underlayer a final glaze

options.text: A later repair, applied after the picture to mend losses in the original surface
options.misconception: reads the layer as a later repair

options.text: The varnish, left deliberately unpainted so the panel would breathe
options.misconception: treats the layer as a deliberately applied varnish

questions.explanation: A monochrome underpainting lies beneath the finished colours and is exposed wherever the upper layers have been lost, which matches what the losses show. A glaze, a repair or a varnish would sit above or within the colour layer, not beneath it.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the colour layer it lies on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the working rule implied by a wall painted over many days.
questions.stem: First, a site survey records that a wall painting was begun on a day in late June and completed in eleven further working days. Second, the painter must plan the schedule. Which rule does the evidence indicate was followed?

options.text: The work was painted in day-sized sections so each area of wet lime was finished before it set.
The work was painted in one continuous sheet, since the lime never sets while the wall is sheltered.
options.misconception: claims the plaster never sets in a sheltered room

options.text: The work was painted onto dry plaster that was re-wetted each evening before work resumed.
options.misconception: confuses re-wetting dry plaster with true fresco

options.text: The work was painted in sections sized to the room, since the plaster sets in architectural units.
options.misconception: invents a rule based on room dimensions

questions.explanation: Buon fresco requires the paint to be applied to wet lime, which carbonates as it dries, so each area must be completed within the day it is laid. Sections sized to the room or a single continuous sheet would leave plaster drying out ahead of the painter.
questions.hint: Think about how long wet lime stays workable.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Oil painting before the fifteenth century
questions.learningObjective: Assess the claim that oil painting was invented in the fifteenth century.
questions.stem: A museum label in a survey store claims that oil painting was invented in the north of Europe in the fifteenth century. Which statement best describes the position the evidence supports?

options.text: Oil binders were in use on panel in Europe well before that century, though recipes changed over time.
No oil paint of any kind existed before the fifteenth century anywhere in the world.
options.misconception: accepts an absolute claim of no earlier use

options.text: Oil was used only for furniture before that century and never for pictures.
options.misconception: restricts earlier oil use to furniture only

options.text: Earlier oil use was confined to Asia and did not reach Europe until the fifteenth century.
options.misconception: misplaces earlier oil use entirely outside Europe

questions.explanation: Oil media appear on European panel painting well before the fifteenth century, so the invention story is too simple, though recipes and methods did change. A total absence of oil, a restriction to furniture and an exclusively Asian origin each go beyond the evidence.
questions.hint: Separate the medium's existence from a change in recipe.

questions.topic: Weave and paint film on canvas
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cracked paint film on canvas follows a regular pattern.

stimulus.body: The laboratory report on the surveyed canvas notes a close plain weave with 16 threads per centimetre in the warp and 14 in the weft, and a paint film that has cracked in a regular network.

questions.stem: From the report above, what best explains the regular network of cracks in the paint film?

options.text: The threads and the weave set a regular pattern that the shrinking film follows.
The canvas was folded along its creases when the roll was stored in the depot.
options.misconception: attributes the cracking to storage creases

options.text: The paint was applied too thickly and cracked as it dried unevenly from the top.
options.misconception: explains the network as a simple drying failure

options.text: The weft count differs from the warp count, so the fabric pulled steadily to one side.
options.misconception: misreads the thread counts as the cause of cracking

questions.explanation: A plain weave presents a regular grid to the paint, and as the film shrinks it follows that grid, which produces a regular network of cracks. Folding, thick application and an uneven thread count do not generate a repeated geometric pattern.
questions.hint: Match the shape of the cracks to the structure beneath.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a canvas ground is built up in several thin layers.
questions.stem: In the survey store the conservator must explain why the canvas ground is built in several layers rather than one. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: One thick layer applied to the cloth would shrink as it dried and would pull away from the weave in patches, because the cloth moves underneath it with changes in humidity. Thin layers, each allowed to dry before the next, keep the ground in contact with the support and allow the shrinkage to be shared out. A common size and colour beneath them holds the layers together and keeps the pale ground even across the whole surface.

questions.explanation: A single thick layer would shrink unevenly and lift from the cloth, whereas thin dried layers keep the ground in contact with the support and spread the shrinkage. The size and the coloured underlayer hold the assembly together and keep it even.
questions.hint: Think about how one thick layer would dry.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret gloss and tack readings to judge how far an oil film has cured.
questions.stem: A monitoring record tracks an oil panel daily for 12 days: dull and tacky on day 1, dull and slightly less tacky on day 5, matte and dry to the touch on day 12. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The film has begun to set but is still oxidising, so full curing lies further ahead.
The film is fully cured on day 12, since it is dry to the touch by then.
options.misconception: treats touch-dry as fully cured

options.text: The film has not begun to oxidise, because its gloss has not returned.
options.misconception: links gloss change to absence of oxidation

options.text: The panel has failed, because a loss of gloss always signals a broken binder.
options.misconception: reads the loss of gloss as a binder failure

questions.explanation: A film that is tacky at first, less tacky by day 5 and only dry to the touch at 12 days is still oxidising and has not finished curing. Touch-dry is not fully cured, and neither the loss of gloss nor the falling tack signals a broken binder here.
questions.hint: Ask how long the change in tack keeps going.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Establish the working order of the underpainting and the colour layers.
questions.stem: First, the survey photographs a tempera panel in which the underlayer shows through in the losses and the colours sit above it in thin, opaque strokes. Second, the curator must explain the working order to a visiting class. Which explanation fits?

options.text: The panel was built up from a monochrome underpainting to the finished colours above it.
The colours were painted first and the underlayer added later over the whole panel.
options.misconception: reverses the order of the two layers

options.text: The underlayer is a varnish that the conservator applied during the survey.
options.misconception: invents a modern varnish layer

options.text: Both layers were applied together in a single wet application.
options.misconception: claims the layers were painted at once

questions.explanation: The underlayer is visible where the upper colours have been lost, which places it beneath them, and the thin opaque strokes above confirm the sequence. A later covering layer, a survey varnish or a single wet application cannot produce that evidence.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a wall painting executed on wet lime from its surface character.
questions.stem: A survey of a chapel records that a wall painting sits directly on the plaster and the paint surface is matt throughout, with no film of its own. What does this tell the conservator?

options.text: The painting was most likely executed in water-based pigment on wet lime plaster.
The painting was executed in oil on dry plaster, since oil on lime gives a matt surface.
options.misconception: attributes a matt surface to oil on dry plaster

options.text: The chapel has no original wall painting and the surface is a later plain wash.
options.misconception: jumps to the conclusion that no painting exists

options.text: The wall was painted in tempera on dry plaster and has simply lost its varnish.
options.misconception: invents a lost varnish to explain the matt surface

questions.explanation: A matt, integrated surface sitting directly on the plaster points to pigment applied in water to wet lime, which bonds as the wall carbonates. Oil on dry plaster keeps its own sheen, and neither a plain wash nor a lost varnish explains the integration.
questions.hint: Ask whether the paint is a film or part of the wall.

questions.topic: Oil painting before the fifteenth century
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about early oil media from a dated panel.

stimulus.body: The catalogue note records an oil-bound panel dated to the early fourteenth century from a small northern church, with a warm translucent glaze over an underlayer of tempera.

questions.stem: From the catalogue note above, what does the early date of the oil-bound panel suggest?

options.text: That oil media were in use on European panel painting well before the fifteenth century.
That the panel must be a later copy made in the fifteenth century.
options.misconception: explains the date by assuming a later copy

options.text: That oil was only ever used as a varnish in the earlier period.
options.misconception: reduces early oil use to varnish alone

options.text: That the underlayer proves the whole panel was finished in tempera.
options.misconception: lets the underlayer override the binding evidence

questions.explanation: A securely dated fourteenth-century oil panel shows the medium was in use on European panels well before the fifteenth century, so later recipes represent development rather than invention. The presence of a tempera underlayer does not change the binder of the upper film.
questions.hint: Read the date against the medium actually present.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weave and paint film on canvas
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a canvas painting must be stored rolled rather than folded.
questions.stem: During a survey of a tented collection the conservator explains why a canvas painting must be stored rolled rather than folded. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Canvas moves with the changes in temperature and humidity of the store, expanding and contracting as it takes up and loses moisture, and a fold is a permanent set that cannot relax back out. A fold concentrates that movement at the crease and adds a stress that the paint film, which is stiffer than the cloth beneath it, cannot follow. Rolling distributes the strain around a wide cylinder instead, and the canvas can still relax when the conditions change.

questions.explanation: Canvas expands and contracts with humidity, and a permanent fold concentrates that movement and adds stress the stiffer paint film cannot follow. Rolling spreads the strain around a broad cylinder so the panel can still relax as conditions change.
questions.hint: Think about the difference between a fold and a roll.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the proportion of chalk in a canvas ground sample.
questions.stem: A survey laboratory weighs a sample of a canvas ground at 2.4 grams, of which 1.2 grams is chalk. What percentage of the ground by weight is chalk?
questions.explanation: Chalk makes up 1.2 of the 2.4 gram sample, which is exactly half, so the ground is 50 percent chalk by weight. Doubling the chalk figure or reading the glue as the chalk share each give the wrong proportion.
questions.hint: Divide the chalk mass by the mass of the whole sample.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a consistent count of joins in tempera panels.
questions.stem: Four tempera panels are recorded with 38, 41, 39 and 40 visible joins per square metre of painted surface. What does that consistency suggest?

That all four panels were painted within a single afternoon of work.

options.text: That the panels were repaired along a grid before they were photographed.
options.misconception: explains the joins as later repairs

options.misconception: confuses joins with the weave texture

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Choose environmental conditions that assist the curing of an oil film.
questions.stem: First, the store's environmental log shows the relative humidity rising from 45 to 65 percent over a week while the oil panels are drying. Second, the keeper must decide how to manage that week. Which decision is best supported?

options.text: Maintain warm, dry, ventilated conditions, since oil cures by oxidation and those conditions assist it.
Seal the room completely, since the panels need protection from every draught.
options.misconception: confuses protection with the cure conditions

options.text: Raise the humidity further, since damp air makes the oil film set harder and faster.
options.misconception: claims damp air accelerates the cure

options.text: Move the panels into a cold store, since cold keeps oil paint from changing at all.
options.misconception: claims cold arrests the oil cure entirely

questions.explanation: Oil cures by taking up oxygen, which proceeds best in warm, dry, well-ventilated air, so a week of damp closed air will hold the films at a tacky stage. Sealing the room, adding damp and cold all work against the chemistry of the cure.
questions.hint: Think about what the curing process needs from the air.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define the practice of blocking in a design.
questions.stem: A curator explains that the panel was blocked in before the colours were added. What does blocking in mean?

options.text: Laying the design in monochrome to fix the light and dark masses of the whole picture.
Making a small trial panel to test the palette before the main work is begun.
options.misconception: confuses blocking in with a colour trial

options.text: Framing the picture in a wooden frame before the painting was started.
options.misconception: gives blocking a carpentry meaning

options.text: Building up the paint in thick layers until the surface is completely level.
options.misconception: reads blocking as a technical build-up

questions.explanation: Blocking in means establishing the composition and its tonal masses in a single monochrome layer before any colour is applied. A colour trial, a frame and a build-up of thick paint are different operations entirely.
questions.hint: Think about the first layer that fixes the composition.

questions.learningObjective: Infer the working method from horizontal bands in a wall.

stimulus.body: The survey records that the wall was plastered in horizontal bands of about 1.5 metres, and that the paint stops cleanly at the upper edge of each band, leaving the plaster above it a different tone.

questions.stem: From the survey note above, what do the horizontal bands tell the conservator?

options.text: That the wall was plastered and painted in day-sized sections, each finished while its lime was wet.
That the wall was built up in courses, so the masonry itself is visible beneath the paint.
options.misconception: reads the bands as masonry courses

options.text: That the painting was transferred from another wall in horizontal strips.
options.misconception: invents a transfer from another surface

options.misconception: describes re-wetting of dry plaster

questions.explanation: Bands that stop the paint cleanly and show a change of plaster tone are the joints between sections laid and painted on different days, each completed within its own hours of wet lime. Masonry courses, a transfer and re-wetting of dry plaster would not leave that pattern.
questions.hint: Think about how a day's work on wet lime would end.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Oil painting before the fifteenth century
questions.learningObjective: Explain why early oil panels are much smaller than later paintings.
questions.stem: During the expedition the curator must explain why the early oil panels are much smaller than the later paintings. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Before the fifteenth century the panel and its wooden frame were usually made by the same workshop that prepared the ground, and both were sized to the painter's working habits rather than to a large room. The narrow panels also suited the panel-maker's tools and the binder's slow drying, since a large area of fresh oil paint could not be managed in one session. Large multi-panel paintings became possible only as binders and workshop practice developed.

questions.explanation: Early oil panels were modest in size because the workshop's tools, its panel-making and the slow setting of the binder all limited the area that could be handled at once. Larger paintings became practical only as the technique and the workshop organisation changed.
questions.hint: Think about what a workshop could manage in a sitting.

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose an unsuitable sizing level from the behaviour of a flaking ground.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a wet-plaster painting cannot be corrected once the lime has set.
questions.stem: A survey team asks why a wall painting made on wet plaster cannot be corrected once the lime has set. Explain the reason.

answer.exemplar: In buon fresco the pigment is carried in water into a bed of wet lime, and it is locked in place by the carbonation of that lime as the wall dries. That reaction is a chemical change in the plaster itself, so the colour becomes part of the wall surface rather than a film sitting on it. Once the lime has carbonated there is nothing to lift and correct, and any attempt to redo the passage means removing the wall surface along with the paint.

questions.explanation: The pigment becomes part of the wall as the wet lime carbonates, so there is no separate film to lift or adjust once the plaster has set. Correcting a passage then means cutting back into the wall surface itself.
questions.hint: Think about whether there is a film to remove.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the area of an early oil panel.
questions.stem: A survey records that an early oil panel measured 74 by 52 centimetres. What is its area in square centimetres?
questions.explanation: The area of the panel is 74 times 52, which is 3,848 square centimetres. Adding the two sides would give 126, which is a perimeter rather than an area and would not describe the panel.
questions.hint: Multiply the two side lengths together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weave and paint film on canvas
questions.learningObjective: Compare canvases to judge which supports a surface paint film.
questions.stem: A survey of a collection records two panels. Panel A has an open loose weave with 9 threads per centimetre and paint that has sunk into the cloth. Panel B has a tight weave with 22 threads per centimetre and paint sitting cleanly on the surface. Which conclusion fits?

options.text: A finer, tighter weave gives a better keyed surface for the paint film than a coarse open one.
The thread counts prove that panel B was painted with a different binder.
options.misconception: infers a binder change from thread counts

options.text: The differences show that panel A was painted on a different continent.
options.misconception: reads weave density as proof of origin

options.text: The thread counts have no bearing on how the paint sits on the cloth.
options.misconception: denies any link between weave and paint adhesion

questions.explanation: The tighter weave of panel B offers a finer and better keyed texture that holds a surface film, while the open weave of panel A lets paint sink between the threads. Thread counts say nothing about the binder, the place of painting, and they do matter for adhesion.
questions.hint: Ask what the weave does for the paint film.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the quantity of size needed for a canvas of given area.
questions.stem: First, the store's survey measures a canvas 1.2 metres by 0.9 metres. Second, the keeper must order size at 25 grams per square metre. How many grams of size are needed?

options.text: 27 grams, because 1.08 square metres times 25 grams gives 27
2.1 metres, because the two side lengths are added before converting
options.misconception: adds the sides instead of finding the area

options.text: 27 kilograms, because the rate per square metre has been converted to grams
options.misconception: confuses grams with kilograms in the total

options.text: 22.5 grams, because the width of 0.9 metres is used as the area
options.misconception: uses one side as though it were the area

questions.explanation: The canvas covers 1.2 times 0.9, which is 1.08 square metres, and 1.08 times 25 grams is 27 grams of size. Adding the sides, converting the unit wrongly or using one side as the area each give a wrong order.
questions.hint: Find the area first, then apply the rate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why tempera panels show a smoother surface than oil panels.
questions.stem: A survey team asks why the tempera panels in the store are so smooth compared with the oil panels. Which explanation fits?

options.text: Tempera sets almost at once, so strokes cannot blend into one another the way oil can.
Tempera is mixed with a filler that levels the brush marks automatically.
options.misconception: invents a filler in the tempera paint

options.text: The panels were polished with an abrasive stone after the paint had dried.
options.misconception: invents a polishing step on tempera panels

options.text: Tempera contains no pigment at all, so only the ground colour is visible.
options.misconception: claims the paint has no pigment in it

questions.explanation: Because tempera sets almost immediately, one stroke cannot be worked into the next and the joins stay visible, giving the smooth, separate-stroke surface seen here. A filler, a polishing step and an absence of pigment would each leave a different trace.
questions.hint: Think about how a stroke can be worked into its neighbour.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the long wait before varnishing an oil painting.

stimulus.body: The field team recorded that the panel was painted in thin layers, each left for several weeks, and that the final varnish was applied only after the last layer had been left to cure for a further year.

questions.stem: From the field record above, why did the team wait a further year before varnishing?

options.text: Because the oil binder needs many months to finish curing and give off its solvent.
Because varnish was only allowed on panels that had been cleaned with solvent first.
options.misconception: invents a cleaning requirement for varnishing

options.text: Because the panel had to settle in the depot so that it reached the room's moisture level.
options.misconception: reduces the wait to acclimatisation of the panel

options.text: Because the pigments settle out of the oil over a year and must be stirred back in.
options.misconception: claims pigments settle out within the paint film

questions.explanation: Oil films continue to oxidise and to release solvent for many months, and a varnish applied before that has finished traps the mobile material and produces a sticky or crazed surface. Acclimatisation and pigment settling do not account for the long wait.
questions.hint: Think about what is still leaving the film.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an underpainting was worked in monochrome rather than in colour.
questions.stem: At the survey store, the conservator explains why the underpainting was made in monochrome rather than in colour. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The point of the first layer is to settle the composition and the distribution of light and dark before any hue is committed, and working in a single monochrome makes every decision visible and easy to judge, since no colour can flatter or disguise an awkward passage of drawing. Once the masses and the modelling are agreed, the coloured layers can be built on a firm foundation, and the picture can be adjusted overall without stripping colour back to the start.

questions.explanation: Working in monochrome settles the composition and the light and dark masses without any colour flattering or hiding a weak passage, so the picture can be judged before hues are committed. The colour work then builds on an agreed foundation.
questions.hint: Think about what the first layer must settle before colour arrives.

questions.topic: Oil painting before the fifteenth century
questions.learningObjective: Compare an early and a later oil panel to identify stages of technique.
questions.stem: In the collection, the survey finds two panels: an early fourteenth-century panel with thin translucent glazes over a stiff tempera-like underlayer, and a later panel with thicker, more freely blended oil paint. What does this contrast suggest?

options.text: The earlier panel belongs to a stage when oil was used in combination with other binders.
The earlier panel is a nineteenth-century imitation of an old painting.
options.misconception: explains the contrast by forgery

options.text: Both panels were made in the same workshop on the same day.
options.misconception: claims the contrast proves a single origin

options.text: The later panel is a copy of the earlier one in a more fashionable technique.
options.misconception: makes the later panel a copy without evidence

questions.explanation: A thin oil glaze over a stiff underlayer points to an early stage in which oil was used with other binders, while the later freer handling reflects a more developed oil technique. Dating, forgery and copying would each require evidence the survey does not report.
questions.hint: Ask what the two-layer structure of the early panel implies.

questions.learningObjective: Convert a canvas measurement into a count of warp threads.
questions.stem: First, the survey measures a canvas 3.5 metres wide with 14 threads per centimetre in the warp. Second, the keeper must estimate how many warp threads cross that width. What is the estimate?

options.text: 4900 threads, because 350 centimetres times 14 threads gives 4900
490 threads, because the metre is used directly in the calculation
options.misconception: fails to convert metres into centimetres

options.text: 350 threads, because the width alone sets the thread count
options.misconception: ignores the thread density entirely

options.text: 25 threads, because the width is divided by the thread count
options.misconception: divides the width by the density

questions.explanation: The width must be converted to centimetres, giving 350, and 350 times 14 threads per centimetre gives 4,900 warp threads. Using metres, ignoring the density or dividing by it each produce a figure the survey cannot support.
questions.hint: Convert the width to centimetres before counting.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what the sizing layer contributes to a canvas support.
questions.stem: A visitor asks what the sizing layer on a survey canvas actually does. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It fills and binds the open weave so that the ground sits on the cloth.
It adds colour to the cloth so the finished picture has a warm tone underneath.
options.misconception: gives the sizing a colouring job

options.text: It makes the canvas stiff enough to carry a very thick layer of oil paint.
options.misconception: claims the size is there to stiffen the cloth

options.text: It stops the cloth from ever absorbing moisture while it hangs on the wall.
options.misconception: treats the size as a moisture barrier

questions.explanation: Sizing soaks into the threads and closes the open weave so the ground is supported by the cloth rather than falling through it. Tinting, stiffening and waterproofing are not what the size accomplishes.
questions.hint: Think about the open spaces between the threads.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Connect the working time of tempera to a recorded schedule.

stimulus.body: The field laboratory records that the tempera on the panel was mixed with a small amount of wine and that the painter's ledgers mention that the panel was completed in a single morning.

questions.stem: From the laboratory and ledger notes above, what is the practical significance of the fast-setting tempera for the painter?

options.text: The work had to be planned and completed in one session, since corrections are impossible once set.
The wine made the paint slow-drying, so the painter had many hours to correct it.
options.misconception: claims the wine slows the setting of tempera

options.text: The wine preserved the panel, so the work could be left unfinished for months.
options.misconception: reads the wine as a preservative

options.text: The tempera was used only for the ground, and the picture was painted in oil.
options.misconception: invents an oil picture over a tempera ground

questions.explanation: Because tempera sets almost at once, a panel has to be designed and completed within the hours it remains workable, which matches the single morning in the ledger. The wine did not slow the set, preserve the panel or turn the picture into an oil painting.
questions.hint: Link the setting time to the recorded working day.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why oil paintings need a long settling period before varnishing.
questions.stem: In the survey store the conservator explains why the oil-painted panels need months of settling before they are varnished. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Oil paint does not dry by evaporation but by oxidation, as the binder combines with oxygen in the air and gradually hardens into a film. The early stages of that set are soft and vulnerable, and solvents continue to be released from the film for many months. Varnishing too early would trap that mobile material and later produce a sticky or crazed surface, so the panel must be left to settle in a ventilated room first.

questions.explanation: Oil hardens by oxidation with the air rather than by losing water, and it keeps giving off solvent for months after it first feels dry. Varnishing at that stage would trap the mobile material and produce a sticky surface later.
questions.hint: Think about how the binder actually hardens.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read plaster joints as evidence of the working method.
questions.stem: A survey of a wall records the plaster joints: the surface is divided by areas whose edges show a straight line of transition from wet to dry lime. What does this record show?

options.text: The wall was painted in day-sized sections, each laid and finished while its lime was wet.
The wall was painted in one single pass, and the joints are later repair cracks.
options.misconception: explains the joints as later repair cracks

options.text: The wall was painted on dry plaster that was re-wetted before each day's work.
options.misconception: reads the joints as evidence of re-wetting dry plaster

options.text: The wall was never painted, and the joints are marks of the original brick courses.
options.misconception: denies any painting on the wall

questions.explanation: Straight edges where wet lime meets dry lime are the joints between day-sized sections, each finished within the hours its plaster stayed workable. A single pass, re-wetting of dry plaster or bare masonry would not leave such transitions.
questions.hint: Ask what a straight wet-to-dry edge means.

questions.topic: Oil painting before the fifteenth century
questions.learningObjective: Infer workshop organisation from a guild inscription.
questions.stem: First, the survey records a panel from the early fourteenth century with an inscription naming a guild of painters. Second, the curator must explain what that suggests about the making of the panel. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: That the work was produced within an organised workshop of recognised craftspeople.
That the panel was made by a single unnamed amateur working entirely alone.
options.misconception: draws isolation from the guild reference

options.text: That the inscription proves the panel was painted in the fifteenth century.
options.misconception: uses a guild inscription to force a later date

options.text: That the guild supplied the panel but left the painting to a commercial dealer.
options.misconception: invents a dealer who painted the panel

questions.explanation: A guild reference places the work within an organised workshop tradition of trained makers, which is how early panel painting was produced. It does not imply solitary amateur work, a fifteenth-century date or a dealer who painted the panel.
questions.hint: Think about what an organised body of painters implies.

questions.topic: Weave and paint film on canvas
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of painting the reverse of a canvas.
questions.stem: A curator is told that the canvas on the survey panel was painted on the reverse as well as on the face. What advantage does that give the object?

options.text: It stiffens the panel and reduces how much the weave and ground can move.
It makes the picture waterproof, because the two films close the weave completely.
options.misconception: claims two films make the cloth waterproof

options.text: It doubles the area of the picture, since both sides carry the same design.
options.misconception: assumes a painted reverse doubles the image

options.text: It removes the need for a separate backing, because the reverse replaces the support.
options.misconception: claims the reverse acts as a structural backing

questions.explanation: Paint on the reverse ties the loose weave and ground into a single stiffened shell, which reduces flexing and the resulting cracking of the picture surface. It does not waterproof the cloth, double the image or replace a backing.
questions.hint: Think about what two painted faces do to the cloth.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a size is allowed to dry before the ground is laid.

stimulus.body: The survey laboratory records that the size on the canvas was applied as a diluted rabbit-skin glue at one part to eight of water, and that the ground was laid on the following day once the size had gone clear.

questions.stem: According to the laboratory record above, why was the size left to go clear before the ground was laid?

options.text: So the size could soak into and dry in the cloth, forming an even keyed film.
So the ground would bond to the size rather than to the cloth fibres.
options.misconception: mislabels the layer the ground actually grips

options.text: So the water could evaporate and take any remaining glue with it.
options.misconception: claims the drying removes the glue from the size

options.text: So the canvas could be stretched on the frame while the size was still soft.
options.misconception: invents a stretching step for the drying size

questions.explanation: A size that has soaked in and dried forms an even film within the weave, ready to key the ground to the cloth. The ground grips that keyed film, and waiting does not remove the glue or prepare the cloth for stretching.
questions.hint: Think about where the size has to end up.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the hatched handling typical of egg tempera.
questions.stem: In the survey store a visitor asks why the tempera panel shows fine hatching rather than smooth blended transitions. Explain the reason.

answer.exemplar: Egg tempera sets within minutes of being laid, so a brush stroke cannot be softened into the neighbouring passage after the first lines are down; it would drag and lift the half-set film rather than blend with it. The painter therefore models form with many small strokes laid side by side, crossing in the shadows and thinning to single lines in the lights. The hatched texture is a direct consequence of the material refusing to be worked once it has begun to set.

questions.explanation: Because a stroke cannot be blended into a passage that has already begun to set, tempera form is built from many small strokes laid beside and across one another. That refusal to be worked is what produces the hatched surface.
questions.hint: Think about what happens if a stroke is worked after it has set.

questions.hint: Count the days from the first date to the second.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the working stage from the flatness of an exposed layer.
questions.stem: A survey team examines a tempera panel in which, where paint is missing, the surviving layer is a flat grey-brown with no modelling of the figures. Which stage does this evidence point to?

options.text: The first blocking stage, before the modelling and the coloured passages were added.
The final stage, in which the whole picture was completed in a single monochrome.
options.misconception: reads the flat layer as a finished monochrome picture

options.text: A layer of dirt that settled in the hollows of the finished paint.
options.misconception: explains the layer as embedded dirt

options.text: A later overpaint applied to disguise the original drawing.
options.misconception: invents a later disguise layer

questions.explanation: A flat, unmodelled layer exposed in the losses is the first block-in, laid before the modelling and colours were worked onto it. A finished monochrome picture, embedded dirt and a disguise layer would each show something the record does not report.
questions.hint: Ask how much work the exposed layer shows.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a loss that follows the outline of a painted figure.
questions.stem: First, the survey records that a wall painting has a loss exactly following the outline of a figure's raised arm, and the plaster within the outline is a different colour from the rest. Second, the conservator must interpret the loss. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: The painter omitted that figure from the day's section and returned to it later.
The figure was painted last and has simply faded more than the surrounding paint.
options.misconception: attributes a sectional loss to fading

options.text: The arm was painted on dry plaster and has fallen away in a single piece.
options.misconception: explains the loss as a dry-plaster detachment

options.text: The outline was a later tracing line made when the wall was surveyed.
options.misconception: invents a survey tracing to explain the shape

questions.explanation: A loss that follows one figure's outline and sits on differently coloured plaster is the mark of a section the painter left unfinished and returned to later. Fading, a dry-plaster detachment and a survey tracing would not respect the figure's contour in that way.
questions.hint: Ask what the outline of the loss corresponds to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Oil painting before the fifteenth century
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the fifteenth century marks development rather than invention in oil painting.
questions.stem: A guide asks why it is misleading to say that oil painting was invented in the fifteenth century. Which statement gives the best answer?

options.text: Oil binders were already used on European panels before that century, though recipes changed.
Because oil was discovered only in the nineteenth century and dated wrongly.
options.misconception: moves the invention to a much later century

options.text: Because oil painting was practised everywhere before that century without exception.
options.misconception: overstates the early use as universal

options.text: Because the fifteenth century is when the word oil was first used in documents.
options.misconception: ties the date to a word rather than a practice

questions.explanation: Oil media appear on European panels well before the fifteenth century, so that century marks a development of technique and recipe rather than an invention. A late discovery, universal earlier use and a matter of vocabulary each misdescribe the evidence.
questions.hint: Separate the medium from a change in recipe.

questions.topic: Weave and paint film on canvas
questions.learningObjective: Predict the effect of an irregular canvas weave on the picture surface.

stimulus.body: The survey notes that the canvas has an irregular hand, with threads that vary slightly in thickness and a line of knots running close to one selvedge.

questions.stem: From the note above, what is the likely effect of this irregular canvas on the picture surface?

options.text: The uneven threads leave a faint irregular texture showing through the paint.
The knots would hold the paint and prevent any cracking in the film.
options.misconception: claims the knots reinforce the paint film

options.text: The irregular hand means the paint will bind less well to the cloth.
options.misconception: confuses an irregular weave with a poorly sized one

options.text: The canvas will stretch unevenly in the frame and pull the picture out of shape.
options.misconception: predicts distortion that an irregular hand does not cause

questions.explanation: An irregular hand leaves small changes in surface level that read faintly through a thin film, which is what the note implies. Knots and thread variation do not reinforce the film, spoil the adhesion, or pull the picture out of shape.
questions.hint: Think about how a surface texture reads through paint.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the size must be applied before the ground and not afterwards.
questions.stem: During the survey, the conservator must explain why the size is applied before the ground and never afterwards. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Sizing has to reach into the weave while the cloth is still open, so that it can form an even film of glue inside the threads and close the passages that would otherwise swallow the ground. Once the ground and the paint are on, no size can get to those threads without passing through the paint film, and a size applied at that stage would sit on top instead of inside. The order is therefore a structural requirement of the panel rather than a matter of convenience.

questions.explanation: Size must penetrate the open weave to form a film inside the threads before the ground goes on; applied afterwards it would merely sit on the paint. The order is structural, not a matter of convenience.
questions.hint: Think about where the size has to reach.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a drying sequence recorded in a sealed container.
questions.stem: A survey records the drying of a small oil test panel in a sealed box: at 48 hours the surface is firm and matt, at 6 months it is slightly tacky again, at 2 years it is hard and the test cloth no longer lifts. Which conclusion fits?

options.text: The film was starved of oxygen in the sealed box and softened as it later took it up.
The panel had spoiled, because oil paint should never become tacky again.
options.misconception: reads a re-tacky film as spoilage

options.text: The panel was too thickly painted, so the surface dried unevenly from the top down.

options.misconception: claims the sealed box caused moisture swell

The picture was finished in monochrome and colour was added in a later campaign.

options.misconception: reverses the working order of the layers

options.misconception: treats the layer as a repair filling

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain a wall scheme that covers only the lower part of a bay.
questions.stem: A survey of a corridor records that the lower part of the wall painting survives but the upper part is bare plaster. Which explanation fits the record?

options.text: The upper wall was never plastered or painted, so the scheme was designed for a lower band.
The upper wall was painted and then washed off with water by later occupants.
options.misconception: invents a deliberate washing away of the painting

options.text: The upper wall was painted in oil, so it flaked away and left bare plaster.
options.misconception: assigns the loss to a different medium

options.text: The upper wall was painted over dry plaster, so it never bonded and fell away.
options.misconception: blames a dry support for a loss of this kind

questions.topic: Oil painting before the fifteenth century
questions.learningObjective: Read a dated panel with several layers for evidence about early oil media.

stimulus.body: The catalogue describes a panel dated to 1380, built of poplar boards with a chalk ground, carrying thin oil glazes, and overpainted in egg tempera at some later date.

questions.stem: From the catalogue description above, what does the panel show about the use of oil media?

options.text: That oil glazes were in use on European panels in the later fourteenth century.
That the oil glazes were added after the tempera overpaint was made.
options.misconception: reverses the order of the two treatments

options.text: That the chalk ground proves the panel was prepared for tempera rather than oil.
options.misconception: claims the ground settles the choice of binder

options.text: That the panel cannot be dated to 1380 because oil was not yet in use.
options.misconception: accepts the invention story against the catalogue

questions.explanation: A securely dated panel carrying oil glazes over a chalk ground shows oil media in use on European panels in the later fourteenth century. The tempera overpaint is later, the ground does not decide the binder, and the catalogue date is not invalidated by the presence of oil.
questions.hint: Read the sequence of the layers against the date.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weave and paint film on canvas
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a canvas ground is normally lighter than the finished picture.
questions.stem: During the visit, the curator explains why the canvas ground is normally lighter than the finished picture. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The ground is a pale reflective layer that establishes the brightness of the lights and shows through wherever the paint is thin, so if it were dark the whole picture would sit on a sombre key and the final colours would have to fight it. Laying the darks in first and the lights over them keeps the palette luminous, and it also means that a loss of paint exposes a coloured layer rather than a dead black patch.

questions.explanation: A pale ground gives the picture its luminous key and receives the darks laid over it, and if it were lost the painter would have to rebuild the lights from nothing. It also means a loss in the surface exposes a coloured layer rather than a dead dark patch.
questions.hint: Think about what the ground does for the lights.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the amount of glue in a batch of size.
questions.stem: A survey laboratory mixes a size at 1 part glue to 6 parts water, and the batch totals 700 millilitres. How many millilitres of glue does the batch contain?
questions.explanation: The ratio gives 7 parts in all, and 700 divided by 7 is 100, so the batch contains 100 millilitres of glue. Adding the ratio instead of dividing by the total parts would confuse the parts with the volume.
questions.hint: Find the total number of parts, then divide.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare stroke counts to distinguish tempera handling from oil handling.
questions.stem: A survey counts distinct brush strokes. One tempera panel shows 210 strokes per square decimetre, and an adjacent oil panel of the same subject shows 60. What does the comparison indicate?

options.text: That the tempera was built from many small separate strokes rather than blended passages.
That the tempera panel was painted by a less practised hand than the oil panel.
options.misconception: attributes the count to skill rather than material

options.text: That the oil panel has lost paint, reducing its apparent stroke count.
options.misconception: invents loss on the oil panel to explain the count

options.text: That the two panels were painted with the same brush and the same method.
options.misconception: assumes identical method despite different counts

questions.explanation: A high stroke count in tempera and a low one in oil matches the fact that tempera sets before strokes can be blended while oil can be worked smoothly. Skill, loss on the oil panel and an identical method do not explain the difference.
questions.hint: Ask what the material allows the painter to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Choose a varnishing schedule that suits the curing of oil paint.
questions.stem: First, the survey records that an oil panel was completed in June, and the store can varnish it either in September or the following March. Second, the curator must choose. Which schedule is better supported?

options.text: The following March, because the films will have had months to give off their solvents.
September, because the surface will be hard enough to take any dust that settles.
options.misconception: prioritises surface hardness over full curing

options.text: September, because varnish applied early stops the panel from cracking in winter.
options.misconception: invents a protective role for early varnish

options.text: The following March, because varnish only adheres properly in cold weather.
options.misconception: ties varnish adhesion to cold weather

questions.explanation: The oil keeps releasing solvent for months after it first feels dry, so a March varnish sits on a film that has largely finished curing, while a September one may trap mobile material. Hardness to the touch, winter protection and cold-weather adhesion are not the relevant points.
questions.hint: Think about how long the film needs to give off solvent.
